turns.text: What Computers Can't Do, first appearing in 1972, opens a new view of the humanities of AI: what does “Hubert Dreyfus criticized reducing human intelli” really mean?
Hubert Dreyfus criticized reducing human intelligence to symbol processing, emphasizing common sense, embodied experience and situated understanding.
It may sound like a small detail, but how does “What Computers Can't Do” support What Computers Can't Do's view of artificial intelligence?
The work or theory turns artificial making, autonomous action or computation into questions about agency, understanding and social order.
What Computers Can't Do left more than a reputation behind. What did later thinkers actually inherit from “What Computers Can't Do”?
Researchers generally treat this node as an important cultural reference in AI humanities rather than a direct prediction of modern technology.
What Computers Can't Do matters not only for what it said then, but for the continuing doorway it left open around “What Computers Can't Do”.
